 Sensor Selection Criteria: 6 Essential Factors to Weigh

 The best performing sensor on paper is not automatically the right choice for a given process.

 Here are the six factors worth weighing first, and why chasing top accuracy everywhere quietly drains a maintenance budget.

 
 Sensor Selection Criteria 
 Accuracy 
 Reliability 
 Range 
 




 Sensor Selection Criteria come down to a simple tradeoff, better performance almost always costs more to buy and more to maintain, so the goal is matching a sensor to what the process actually needs.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn the main Sensor Selection Criteria engineers weigh before specifying a device, and why the highest performing option is not always the correct one.


 We will cover accuracy, repeatability, range, reliability, linearity, and cost, along with process environment protection, response time, and safety considerations that apply across almost any sensor type.


 
 
 
 6 Core Sensor Selection Criteria to Weigh First


 The greater the performance requirement, the higher the purchase and maintenance cost, so these six factors are usually weighed together rather than one at a time.


 
 
 1

 Accuracy

 How closely a measured value matches the true value, usually stated as a maximum error in engineering units or as a percentage of range.

 

 
 2

 Repeatability

 How consistent the same measurement comes out across repeated trials under identical conditions, approached from the same direction each time.

 

 
 3

 Range

 The lower and upper measurement limits a sensor covers, with wider ranges generally trading away some accuracy and reproducibility.

 

 
 4

 Reliability

 The probability a sensor keeps performing correctly over its intended service period, more critical wherever a failure risks safety or product quality.

 

 
 5

 Linearity

 How closely the sensor's output tracks a straight line against the true process variable across its full range.

 

 
 6

 Cost

 Total cost across purchase, installation, wiring, documentation, operation, and every year of maintenance over the sensor's working life.

 




 
 Did You Know

 A sensor's own linearity error can often be corrected mathematically after the fact, a square root correction for an orifice flow meter or a polynomial fit for a thermocouple, so nonlinearity alone is rarely a reason to reject an otherwise good sensor.

 Reproducibility vs Repeatability, and Why the Difference Matters


 These two terms sound alike but answer different questions, and mixing them up leads to specifying the wrong test during vendor evaluation.


 
 
 Repeatability 
 Consistency across a short run of consecutive measurements taken close together, under conditions that are essentially unchanged from one reading to the next.
